request.user_question: Explain the difference between FRP in MW and energy in GJ.

response.explanation_markdown:
Fire Radiative Power (FRP), reported in megawatts (MW), measures the instantaneous rate of radiant heat output at the moment a satellite observes a thermal anomaly [K1]. Because one megawatt equals one megajoule per second, FRP represents current burning intensity during an individual satellite overpass rather than cumulative heat output [K1]. Such detections indicate activity consistent with probable active burning, but satellite power alone does not confirm a named wildfire or establish its perimeter.

Thermal energy in gigajoules (GJ) represents cumulative fire radiative energy integrated over time across an area [K1]. Because satellites provide discontinuous observations, summing instantaneous FRP readings does not yield total energy [K1]. Deriving energy requires temporal integration of calibrated power over the duration of the event, accounting for satellite coverage and diurnal reconstruction [K1]. This integrated energy total is subsequently used to estimate consumed dry biomass [K6].

citations.title: Fire radiative power and energy
citations.relevance_note: FRP is instantaneous fire radiative power in MW, equivalent to MJ per second. FRE is energy integrated over time in MJ. One GJ is 1000 MJ. Summing instantaneous satellite FRP samples does not give energy. The local scientific energy tool integrates calibrated daily FRE over the cube cells represented each day. Estimates depend on temporal reconstruction and sensor coverage.

citations.title: Biomass and emission estimates
citations.relevance_note: Dry biomass consumed is estimated as 0.368 tonnes per GJ of integrated FRE. PM2.5 needs measured annual fuel classes and supported fuel-specific emission factors; missing or unsupported inputs remain null. CO2 in episode profiles uses an explicitly assumed constant factor, not measured emissions. Energy and biomass do not measure ambient air quality, health impacts, casualties, ecological damage or burned hectares.

request.user_question: When does the typical fire season peak in this area?

In the Sierra Oeste area, the typical fire season peaks in late July, with the long-term mean peak date falling on 26 July (mean peak day of year 207.7) across 24 years of satellite observations from 2001 to 2025. Peak thermal activity shows high seasonal consistency, with a peak consistency score of 0.7345810371347284 and a mean season duration of 172.49052532486076 days. Satellite-detected thermal activity indicates probable active vegetation burning during this mid-summer window rather than confirmation of specific named wildfires. Individual annual peaks commonly concentrate between late July and mid-August, including peak dates of 2021-08-15, 2022-07-19, and 2025-07-25. [K10] [K9]

### Fire season timing

In **Selected Sierra Oeste area**, the burning season typically peaks around **26 Jul** and lasts about **172.5 days**, based on 24 complete years (2001–2025). [6]

### Decadal drift

The peak has moved **2.71 days earlier per decade** (about **6.50 days** across 2001–2025). This trend is not statistically distinguishable from year-to-year variability (p = 0.713).

| Year | Peak burning date | Season duration (days) | Energy (GJ) |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: |
| 2021 | 2021-08-15 | 57.3 | 19,743.104 |
| 2022 | 2022-07-19 | 75.0 | 12,955.319 |
| 2023 | 2023-08-29 | 336.9 | 109.233 |
| 2024 | 2024-08-03 | 286.9 | 134.621 |
| 2025 | 2025-07-25 | 119.1 | 17,343.549 |

The peak date is the energy-weighted centre of each year's fire activity, and duration is its effective seasonal width. A weakly seasonal year gives a long duration and an unstable peak. Only complete calendar years are used.

request.user_question: Which historical 30-day windows had the least thermal activity?

response.explanation_markdown:
Across the 27-year historical record for Sierra Oeste, the 30-day window with the lowest thermal activity runs from March 20 to April 18. During this early spring interval, the mean daily energy density reaches just 0.062 MJ/km², with satellite detections occurring on only 1.41% of days. 

Two other notable quiet periods occur in autumn and mid-winter: October 11 to November 9 averages 0.087 MJ/km² (detections on 1.14% of days), and January 2 to January 31 averages 0.101 MJ/km² (detections on 1.28% of days). By contrast, peak historical burning centers in mid-summer, spanning July 18 to August 16 with an average daily energy density of 222.185 MJ/km². [K4] [K9]

### Historically quiet 30-day windows

In **Selected Sierra Oeste area**, the quietest 30-day window in the 27-year record runs from **20 Mar to 18 Apr**. Fire was detected on **1.4%** of those days, against **7.8%** in the most active window (18 Jul to 16 Aug). [6]

| Window | Mean fire energy density (MJ/km²/day) | Spread from adjacent cells (MJ/km²/day) | Days with detections (%) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 20 Mar to 18 Apr | 0.0616 | 0.0000 | 1.4 |
| 11 Oct to 9 Nov | 0.0873 | 0.0000 | 1.1 |
| 2 Jan to 31 Jan | 0.1010 | 0.0000 | 1.3 |

These windows show when satellites have historically recorded the least fire energy and the least spread between neighbouring cells. They are not a burn authorisation: weather, fuel moisture, staffing and local regulations decide whether a planned burn is safe. Days without a detection are counted as quiet, although cloud can hide activity.

The satellite observations recorded within the selected Sierra Oeste cells demonstrate elevated fire radiative power and persistent heat anomalies consistent with active vegetation burning [K10]. These thermal detections reflect localized radiative energy output integrated across satellite sensor overpasses rather than confirmed on-the-ground perimeters or official containment boundaries [K10].

Any named wildfires reported in nearby municipalities or administrative districts provide regional situational context rather than a confirmed identity for these specific map cells. ### Largest thermal events

The largest recorded event in **Selected Sierra Oeste area** between 2000-11-01 and 2026-11-14 peaked on **2026-07-25**: about **335,090.289 GJ** over **6 days**, or **123,313.226 tonnes** of dry biomass consumed. [1] [6]

request.user_question: Show the yearly sensor breakdown for Terra, Aqua and VIIRS.

response.explanation_markdown:
In the recorded data for Sierra Oeste, active-fire observations are logged for 2026 across Terra, Aqua, and VIIRS instruments, excluding stationary industrial heat sources. For 2026, Terra recorded 6 fire days with a mean energy density of 26,724.88 MJ/km², Aqua logged 9 fire days with a mean energy density of 7,860.76 MJ/km² (yielding a combined MODIS total of 878 raw detections), and VIIRS registered 40 fire days with 9,242 detections and a mean energy density of 1,682.58 MJ/km². 

The higher raw count for VIIRS reflects its finer 375 m spatial resolution and higher thermal sensitivity compared to the 1 km nominal MODIS footprint, rather than an increase in separate physical fire occurrences [K3]. Because raw detection counts vary by sensor geometry and overpass timing, calibrated fire radiative energy (FRE) integrated across the observation area provides the consistent scientific metric for total thermal output.

### Record by sensor

Between 2026 and 2026, **Selected Sierra Oeste area** has **878 MODIS detections** (Terra and Aqua, 1 km) and **9,242 VIIRS detections** (375 m). VIIRS detections begin in **2026** in this selection. [5] [6]

| Year | MODIS detections | VIIRS detections | Terra energy | Aqua energy | VIIRS energy |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 2026 | 878 | 9,242 | 26,724.8847 (6 d) | 7,860.7630 (9 d) | 1,682.5832 (40 d) |

Energy columns give each sensor's calibrated mean daily energy density in MJ/km²/day over the days it recorded fire, with that number of days in brackets. A detection is a satellite thermal anomaly, not a count of distinct fires. VIIRS sees smaller and cooler fires than MODIS, so detection counts are not comparable between sensors or across the years before and after VIIRS; the calibrated energy columns are the comparable quantity. [2] [3]

citations.title: Satellite detections and incident identity
citations.relevance_note: NASA FIRMS detections are satellite thermal anomalies, not a count of distinct fires. A single fire may generate many detections over different sensors and days. Thermal anomalies can also be agricultural burning or industrial sources. A selected polygon or H3 hexagon is a query area, not a confirmed wildfire perimeter. Zero detections do not prove absence of fire: clouds, overpasses, thresholds and archive coverage affect observation. Thermal sensors can detect flaming and sufficiently hot smoldering. A decline in detection counts alone cannot distinguish less combustion from obscuration, sampling or detection thresholds; none of these is a measured explanation without matching evidence.

A regional report is not proof that each selected satellite cell belongs to that incident. A cause absent from retrieved reports is unverified in those reports, not necessarily unknown to authorities.
